Risk of Bias: Random Sequence Generation (Selection Bias): The risk of bias was judged to be low. A random allocation sequence of group codes was generated using permuted blocks of length 16. Two separate randomization lists were created: one for children with baseline haemoglobin (Hb) > 70 g/L and another for children with baseline Hb ≤ 70 g/L. These lists were serially numbered and included allocated treatment codes before any children were enrolled. Allocation Concealment (Selection Bias): The risk of bias was judged to be low. Allocation was concealed from investigators and field personnel until the study was completed and the data were analyzed. Similarity of Baseline Outcome Measurements (Confounding): The risk of bias was judged to be low. Children in both groups were comparable at baseline in terms of haematology and plasma zinc status. Similarity of Baseline Characteristics (Confounding): The risk of bias was unclear. Children in both groups were comparable at baseline for sociodemographic variables. However, it was not clear whether breastfed children were included. Incomplete Outcome Data (Attrition Bias): The risk of bias was unclear. In the fortified milk group, 9 children left the area, 2 children died, and 16 withdrew consent. In the control milk group, 18 children left the area, 2 children died, and 16 withdrew consent. The participant flow chart was not clear. Blinding of Participants and Personnel (Performance Bias): The risk of bias was judged to be low. The study was reported as double-blinded, with both investigators and participants blinded to the intervention. Blinding of Outcome Assessment (Detection Bias): The risk of bias was judged to be low. The study remained blinded until the data were analyzed. Contamination (Performance Bias): The risk of bias was judged to be low. Contamination was unlikely as the supplementation boxes were labeled with the child’s identification information, and the letter code of the supplementation was removed. Selective Reporting (Reporting Bias): The risk of bias was unclear. The study was approved by the Human Research and Ethical Review Committees at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and Annamalai University, India. However, the participant flow was not clearly reported. Other Bias: The risk of bias was unclear. No additional information was provided. Recruitment Bias: The risk of bias was unclear. Stecksén-Blicks 2009 (C): Methods: This was a double-blind, cluster, placebo-controlled randomized controlled trial (RCT) with two arms. Participants: Children aged 1–5 years attending 14 daycare centers with 27 units in northern Sweden were invited and recruited through meetings with parents. Interventions: A total of 248 children were assigned to one of two groups: 1. Group 1 received milk fortified with 1.5 mg fluoride per liter. 2. Group 2 (n = 115, from 10 daycare units) received standard milk (150 mL per day) at lunch. The milk was prepared by daycare staff by adding one color-coded capsule (10 mL) to each liter of milk. The intervention group’s milk contained 1.5 mg fluoride and 10^7 CFU/mL of Lactobacillus rhamnosus LB21 per liter. The control group’s capsules contained only skimmed milk and were identical in appearance except for the color code. Outcomes: The primary outcome was caries increment. Secondary outcomes included measures of general health, such as days with respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms, number of doctor visits, days on antibiotic treatment, days with otitis media, and days with sick leave. Notes: 1. The institutions were located in Norsmalin and Hörnefors, small communities with fewer than 10,000 inhabitants near the city of Umeå in northern Sweden. 2. The intervention was served only on weekdays (at school) and lasted 21 months. 3. The authors reported adjusting for cluster effects. Source of Funding: The study was financially supported by the County Council of Västerbotten (TUA) and the Borrow Foundation, UK. Norrmejerier Ekonomisk Förening, Umeå, Sweden, supported the study by preparing and distributing the milk. Risk of Bias: Random Sequence Generation (Selection Bias): The risk of bias was judged to be low. Daycare centers were randomly assigned to two parallel groups by a staff member at the local dairy using coin tossing. Allocation Concealment (Selection Bias): The risk of bias was judged to be low. Daycare units were referred to as blue or yellow units to conceal their allocation. The code was kept by an independent monitor and was not unveiled until all data were computerized. Similarity of Baseline Outcome Measurements (Confounding): The risk of bias was judged to be low. There were no significant differences in baseline outcomes between groups. Similarity of Baseline Characteristics (Confounding): The risk of bias was judged to be low. There were no significant differences in baseline characteristics between groups. Incomplete Outcome Data (Attrition Bias): The risk of bias was judged to be low. After three months, 58 children left the project because they moved to primary schools, and 4 dropped out for other reasons. Blinding of Participants and Personnel (Performance Bias): The risk of bias was judged to be low. Neither the researchers nor the clinicians, personnel, or families at the daycare centers knew whether the children received control or intervention milk during the study. Blinding of Outcome Assessment (Detection Bias): The risk of bias was unclear. This was not mentioned. Contamination (Performance Bias): The risk of bias was judged to be low. Since randomization was done at the daycare center level, contamination was unlikely to have occurred. Selective Reporting (Reporting Bias): The risk of bias was judged to be low. The study was approved by the research ethics committee at Umeå University (§562/03, dnr 03-475). Other Bias: The risk of bias was unclear. No additional information was provided. Recruitment Bias: The risk of bias was judged to be low. Children were recruited to the trial before the clusters were randomized. Baseline Imbalance: The risk of bias was judged to be low. The intra-cluster correlation coefficient was estimated to reflect the homogeneity of the sample using a one-way ANOVA. Loss of Clusters: The risk of bias was judged to be low. No clusters were lost to follow-up. Incorrect Analysis: The risk of bias was judged to be low. Due to the clustered design, the outcomes in caries and general health were analyzed with age as a covariate in a multilevel logistic regression. Compatibility with Individual RCTs: The risk of bias was judged to be low. The cluster design did not seem to affect the findings of the study.
